cards.title: WebRTC Field Notes
cards.subtitle: A pocket atlas of peer connections, NAT traversal, and the protocols that make real-time media flow.
cards.html:
Volume Senior & Architect Track
Compiled May 2026
Cards Sixteen
Use Pre-interview & design rounds

cards.title: The Four Obstacles
cards.subtitle: WebRTC is one sentence: two browsers want to send UDP packets to each other, but NAT is in the way. Every acronym solves one obstacle on that path.
cards.html:
1. Find each other. A meeting place, agreed in advance. → Signaling   (your WebSocket — not in the WebRTC spec)
  2. Agree on what to speak. Codecs, encryption, transport parameters. → SDP   (offer / answer, exchanged via signaling)
  3. Find a network path. Through NATs and firewalls. → ICE   (uses STUN for discovery, TURN for relay)
  4. Encrypt the media. Mandatory in WebRTC, no plaintext mode. → DTLS → SRTP   (handshake derives keys; SRTP is the wire format)

If you can list the four obstacles, you can always reconstruct the rest.

cards.title: Three Layers Never Conflate
cards.subtitle: Most WebRTC confusion comes from mixing these up. Each layer runs over different infrastructure, with different scaling concerns and different cost lines.
cards.html:
LayerWhat It DoesWho Builds It
Signaling Exchanges SDP and ICE candidates between peers, before media flows. You — typically a WebSocket fleet
NAT traversal Discovers public IPs, finds and validates network paths between peers. STUN & TURN providers, or self-hosted coturn
Media transport Encrypted real-time audio/video/data over UDP. Direct between peers. Browser, end-to-end

Key point. The signaling server is in the path before connection but never carries media. STUN is consulted only at gather time. TURN, when used, carries every byte of media.

cards.title: SDP The Session Blob
cards.subtitle: Session Description Protocol — a plain-text manifest that describes what a peer can speak. Exchanged via offer/answer through your signaling server.
cards.html:
What it carries. Codec list (Opus, VP8, VP9, AV1, H.264), RTP extensions, encryption fingerprints, ICE credentials (ufrag, pwd), bandwidth limits, media stream IDs.

v=0
o=- 4611737293671806839 2 IN IP4 127.0.0.1
s=-
t=0 0
m=audio 9 UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF 111 103 104
a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2
a=fingerprint:sha-256 AB:CD:...
a=ice-ufrag:F7gI
a=ice-pwd:x9cml/YzichV2+XlhiMu8g

Offer / answer rule. The answer must be a subset of the offer. The result is a negotiated session: both peers know the exact codec, encryption, and transport parameters.

cards.title: ICE Gathering Five Steps
cards.subtitle: Interactive Connectivity Establishment — RFC 8445. Doesn't predict the right path; it tries every plausible path in parallel and picks the first that works.
cards.html:
1. Enumerate interfaces. Walk every local interface (WiFi, Ethernet, VPN). Each yields a host candidate.
  2. Query STUN. From each interface, send STUN binding requests. Returns your public IP:port — a server-reflexive (srflx) candidate.
  3. Allocate on TURN. If TURN is configured, request an allocation from each. Returns a relay candidate.
  4. Trickle. Each candidate, as discovered, fires onicecandidate and is sent to the peer through signaling.
  5. Connectivity checks. Both peers pair their local with the remote candidates and run STUN binding pings. The first valid pair (by priority) becomes the selected pair.

cards.title: Three Candidates, One Priority Order
cards.subtitle: ICE prefers the cheapest, most direct path. Falls back only when checks fail. The priority order is the heart of the whole system.
cards.html:
TypeSourcePriority
host Local interface — same LAN, same WiFi, same VPN. Highest
srflx Public IP discovered via STUN. Works through most NATs. Medium
relay Address allocated on a TURN server. Always works, paid path. Lowest

The fourth type. Peer-reflexive (prflx) is discovered during connectivity checks — when a check packet reaches the peer from an address neither side gathered ahead of time, due to NAT behavior. ICE handles this gracefully.

Direct first. Reflexive second. Relay only when nothing else works.

cards.title: STUN discovers. TURN relays.
cards.subtitle: A common confusion: these are not interchangeable. They solve different problems and have wildly different cost profiles.
cards.html:
STUNTURN
RoleTells you your public IPRelays media between peers
Default Port3478 / UDP3478 + 5349 (TLS) + 443 (firewall escape)
StateStatelessStateful — allocations with lifetime
AuthNoneRequired (username + credential, often HMAC time-limited)
BandwidthNegligible (a few packets)Full media bandwidth, both directions
Cost~Free~$0.13 / hour per relayed 720p call
Used by~80% of calls (gather time only)~10–20% of calls (active path)

Why TURN exists. Symmetric NAT assigns a different public port for every destination. The address learned via STUN is valid only for the STUN server. TURN sidesteps this by holding a real public IP both peers can reach.

cards.title: DTLS the keys. SRTP the bytes.
cards.subtitle: All WebRTC media is mandatorily encrypted. There is no plaintext mode; the spec doesn't allow one.
cards.html:
DTLS — Datagram Transport Layer Security. TLS adapted for UDP. Used here for the handshake that derives SRTP encryption keys. The SDP carries DTLS certificate fingerprints so peers can verify each other before any media flows.

SRTP — Secure Real-time Transport Protocol. RTP plus AES encryption plus HMAC authentication. The actual on-the-wire format for every encrypted media packet.

SCTP over DTLS — what RTCDataChannel rides on. Gives you per-channel reliability/ordering choices: TCP-like or UDP-like.

DTLS handshake~150–300 ms
CipherAES-128-GCM (typical)
VerificationSHA-256 fingerprint in SDP

cards.title: Trickle ICE
cards.subtitle: An optimisation over RFC 5245. Peers send the offer immediately and stream candidates as discovered, instead of waiting for full gathering.
cards.html:
Without trickle. Caller calls setLocalDescription, waits 2–5 seconds for all candidates, then sends a fully-baked offer. Setup time: 5–10 seconds.

With trickle. Caller sends offer immediately. Each candidate fires onicecandidate as it's found and is forwarded through signaling. Setup time: under a second.

pc.onicecandidate = (event) => {
  if (event.candidate) {
    signalingChannel.send({
      type: 'candidate',
      candidate: event.candidate
    });
  } else {
    // null candidate = gathering complete
  }
};

Half-trickle. When bridging to systems that don't support trickle (some SIP gateways), gather locally for ~500ms, send what you have in the offer, then trickle the rest.

cards.title: ICE Restart
cards.subtitle: When the network path breaks mid-call — laptop changes WiFi, mobile hands off, VPN connects — the existing candidates may all become invalid. Restart re-runs ICE without tearing down the call.
cards.html:
// Trigger restart on the peer connection
const offer = await pc.createOffer({ iceRestart: true });
await pc.setLocalDescription(offer);
// Send the new offer through signaling
// The peer answers; both sides re-gather and re-check

What's preserved. The DTLS state. The SRTP keys. The peer connection object itself. There's no key renegotiation, no media tear-down.

What's rebuilt. ICE credentials (ufrag, pwd). Candidate gathering. Connectivity checks. The selected pair.

Without restart, network changes silently fail the call.

When to trigger. Detect iceConnectionState === 'disconnected' for more than a few seconds, or use the Network Information API to detect interface changes.

cards.title: Mesh, SFU, MCU
cards.subtitle: Pure peer-to-peer dies past four participants. The choice between SFU and MCU is one of the canonical real-time architecture decisions.
cards.html:
TopologyMechanismUse Case
Mesh (P2P) Every client connects to every other. N-1 uploads per client. 1:1 calls only
SFU Server forwards streams without decoding. ~1–3% CPU per stream. Most modern conferencing — Meet, Jitsi, LiveKit, mediasoup
MCU Server decodes, mixes, re-encodes one composite. ~30–50% CPU per stream, +100–300ms latency. Telephony bridges, low-bandwidth clients

Why mesh fails. Five peers at 720p means ~1.5 Mbps × 4 uploads = 6 Mbps upload per client. Most home connections cap there.

Simulcast. Publisher sends 1080p + 720p + 360p simultaneously; SFU forwards the right resolution to each subscriber. Doubles upload cost but cleanly handles heterogeneous clients.

cards.title: Two State Machines
cards.subtitle: A common bug: assuming gathering=complete means you're connected. They're separate machines tracking different things.
cards.html:
iceGatheringState — am I still finding my own candidates?

new  →  gathering  →  complete

iceConnectionState — have I established a working path with the peer?

new  →  checking  →  connected  →  completed
                  ↘  disconnected
                  ↘  failed
                  ↘  closed

connectionState — the aggregate, including DTLS:

new  →  connecting  →  connected
                    ↘  disconnected / failed / closed

For UI purposes, watch connectionState. For diagnostics, watch the other two.

cards.title: Four Tiers, Independent Scale
cards.subtitle: A production WebRTC system has four scaling tiers. Each scales differently and has its own cost profile. Treating them as one server is the junior answer.
cards.html:
1. Signaling. WebSocket fleet, sticky-sessioned per room. Redis pub/sub or Kafka for cross-node messaging. Cheap to scale; latency-sensitive on connect.
  2. STUN. Stateless, anycast in front. Effectively free. Place close to users.
  3. TURN. Bandwidth-heavy. Region-pin to nearest user. Authentication via short-lived HMAC credentials. The dominant cost line in many deployments.
  4. SFU. Stateful — room ↔ node affinity. Vertical scale per node (CPU + 1 Gbps NIC), horizontal scale via room sharding plus cascading for cross-region rooms.

Capacity math, 100K concurrent users.

SFU node capacity, 720p~600 streams
TURN node capacity, full duplex~300 sessions
TURN nodes needed, 20% relayed~67

cards.title: WebRTC vs WebSocket + PCM
cards.subtitle: For AI voice agents — the canonical choice. Each wins in a different operating regime; the architect's job is knowing which.
cards.html:
DimensionWebSocket + PCMWebRTC
Stack complexityOne connectionSignaling + SFU + TURN
Setup latency~50–200 ms500 ms – 1.5 s
Echo cancellationBuild it yourselfBuilt in
Jitter bufferBuild it yourselfBuilt in
Adaptive bitrateNone — fixed PCMYes (GCC, TWCC)
Bandwidth, voice~256 kbps PCM~16–32 kbps Opus
Backend controlFullMediated by SFU

When WebSocket+PCM wins. One-shot voice agents on good networks. Backend integrations. Anything where you control both ends and want simplicity.

When WebRTC wins. Long-form duplex conversations. Mobile users on varied networks. Full-duplex barge-in. Anywhere call quality needs to degrade gracefully.

Anchor. OpenAI's Realtime API offers both — WebRTC for browsers, WebSocket for backends. Exactly the right call.

cards.title: The 30-Second Pitch
cards.subtitle: If you forget everything else, keep this. It's the whole stack in one paragraph, organised by the four obstacles.
cards.html:
WebRTC is a browser-native standard for peer-to-peer real-time media. Audio and video flow directly between peers as encrypted UDP — SRTP. Setup uses SDP blobs exchanged through a signaling server you build. NAT traversal is handled by ICE, which gathers host, server-reflexive, and relay candidates using STUN and TURN. Encryption keys come from a DTLS handshake. Beyond two peers, production uses an SFU.

One-line memory hook.

Signal the SDP, ICE the path, DTLS the keys, SRTP the bytes.

StepWhat Happens
SignalSDP offer/answer through your WebSocket
ICEGather host → srflx → relay; check pairs; pick one
DTLSHandshake derives SRTP keys; fingerprint verified
SRTPEncrypted media flowing peer-to-peer
